seo.title: Karmic tail 12 22 10 compatibility: what it means for a couple
seo.description: Karmic tail 12 22 10 compatibility: why it exists only for a couple and what The Hanged Man, The Fool and The Wheel of Fortune teach, read through Candide.

title: 12-22-10 in compatibility: the karmic tail only a couple can have
short: No single birth date can produce the triple 12-22-10. In a personal destiny matrix it would need a centre of 2, and no person ever has that centre, so these three numbers appear only in compatibility, when two charts are added together — in roughly one couple out of 269. This is the tail of a couple who can survive any turn of fate and lose their way when fate stops turning. The Hanged Man at the entry is a common language of "let's bear it, it was meant to be". The Fool in the middle is a road on which everything starts again. The Wheel of Fortune in the main task asks them to learn to live not from one turn to the next, but in between.

sections.h2: Candide: the story of a couple taught that all is for the best
paragraphs: On 1 November 1755 an earthquake destroyed Lisbon. Europe had been happily repeating after Leibniz that ours is the best of all possible worlds, and the disaster put the question bluntly: how do ruins fit with the idea that everything is arranged for the best? Voltaire answered three years later with a funny and cruel little novel. Its hero, Candide, grows up in a Westphalian castle and studies under the philosopher Pangloss, who "proved admirably that there is no effect without a cause, and that, in this best of all possible worlds, the Baron's castle was the most magnificent of castles". The teacher's conclusion: "they should have said all is for the best".

The book falls into three acts. In the first, Candide and the Baron's daughter Cunegonde fall in love over Pangloss's lessons, kiss behind a screen and are parted at once: the Baron throws the young man out of the castle. In the second comes a road across half the world, from Westphalia to Paraguay and from Paris to Constantinople, and for almost all of it the lovers are apart. In the third they are together at last, on a small farm by the Propontis, today's Sea of Marmara. That is where the hardest part begins.

The cards of the tail do not promise a couple shipwrecks or earthquakes: the events of the novel are grotesque, and numbers say nothing about events. What matches is something else — the way the characters talk about fate. At the entry to the story stands a common language of waiting and justifying, and that is The Hanged Man. In the middle stands the ability to pull up stakes, and that is The Fool. At the end stands the question of what to do when the wheel has stopped, and that is The Wheel of Fortune.

sections.h2: Entry to the task: a teacher called All-Tongue
paragraphs: The name Pangloss is built from two Greek words: pan, "all", and glossa, "tongue" or "language". Voltaire's commentators point this out, and for a couple's tail it is more than a joke. Point M, where these couples have The Hanged Man, appears twice in a compatibility reading. In the couple's karmic tail it is labelled "Entry to the task", and in the sphere "Relationship and common language" it is labelled "Common language". For Lisovskaya this is the point of a couple's shared wishes and agreements — their "common language". In the novel, the lovers' common language is taught by a man whose name means All-Tongue.

Both grew up on the same lessons. Candide "listened attentively and believed innocently". Cunegonde, having watched Pangloss give the chambermaid "a lesson in experimental natural philosophy" in the shrubbery, returns to the castle "filled with the desire to be learned", dreaming "that she might well be a sufficient reason for young Candide, and he for her". Raison suffisante is Pangloss's favourite term. The declaration of love is made in the teacher's language. From the very start this couple speaks not a language of its own, but a shared one learned at school.

The first scene of their love is already The Hanged Man. The next day after dinner they find themselves behind a screen: a handkerchief, a hand, lips. The Baron passes by and, "beholding this cause and effect chased Candide from the castle with great kicks on the backside". The wish has been named — and in the same minute it is suspended for the rest of the book. From then on Candide does almost everything for Cunegonde: he pays, he ransoms, he searches for her from Surinam to Constantinople. And all that time their union hangs in mid-air.

This is what The Hanged Man looks like at a couple's entry. Lisovskaya's card for this energy has an exact detail: such couples take a long time to enter a relationship, and they need a push from outside to marry. Voltaire makes the push literal: Candide marries when Cunegonde's brother declares that his sister shall only marry a baron of the empire — "the extreme impertinence of the Baron determined him to conclude the match". In real life it shows in small things. The wedding is put off "until we have our own flat", the move "until the promotion", the important conversation "until the holidays". One gives way, the other is grateful, and both call it wisdom. And when something falls through, the couple says in chorus: "it was meant to be".

That language has real strength. In Lisovskaya's reading, The Hanged Man is tact, readiness to give way, the ability to wait and to sense each other at a distance; without it Candide would not have covered half his road. But point M stands on the line of tasks, and Lisovskaya warns that the same wish can turn into resistance. **A common language that explains every loss sooner or later starts explaining inaction too.**

sections.h2: A man upside down: what happened in Lisbon harbour
paragraphs: Voltaire paints the most exact portrait of this trap before the earthquake even begins. In a storm off Lisbon, a sailor knocks down the good Anabaptist James and, from the force of his own blow, "tumbled head foremost overboard, and stuck upon a piece of the broken mast" — in Voltaire's French he "remained suspended" there. The first hanged man of the novel hangs head down. James hauls him up and is thrown into the sea himself. Candide is about to jump after him, "but was prevented by the philosopher Pangloss, who demonstrated to him that the Bay of Lisbon had been made on purpose for the Anabaptist to be drowned".

Here is the mechanism of entry 12 in its minus: the urge to help is there, but the common language gets in first. The explanation of why everything is right arrives at the very moment when action is needed. Among a couple's tasks under The Hanged Man, Lisovskaya names the inability to take responsibility, and Pangloss shows where it comes from: if everything is necessary, nobody is answerable for anything. A few pages later the scene repeats on land. Wounded, Candide lies under the rubble and begs: "get me a little wine and oil; I am dying." Pangloss replies that "this concussion of the earth is no new thing": Lima had the same last year, "the same cause, the same effects". Candide agrees — "Nothing more probable" — and asks again. The philosopher objects: "I maintain that the point is capable of being demonstrated." In a couple this sounds familiar: one says "I feel awful", the other explains why it happened.

Then "the sages of that country could think of no means more effectual to prevent utter ruin than to give the people a beautiful auto-da-fé". Pangloss and Candide are seized together, "the one for speaking his mind, the other for having listened with an air of approbation". These are the two roles in a couple's common language: one formulates, the other nods, and both are answerable. Candide is flogged; Pangloss is hanged, "though that was not the custom". Voltaire's next sentence: "The same day the earth sustained a most violent concussion."

In one scene the first and the last cards of the tail meet. A sacrifice is made to stop the Wheel, and the Wheel keeps turning. In Waite's divinatory list for The Hanged Man, "sacrifice" stands in one row with "divination" and "prophecy": sacrifice, intuition, divination, prophecy. Our reading for this couple is a secret bargain with fate: "if we endure it properly, we will be repaid". Voltaire shows that such a bargain buys nothing.

Benebell Wen describes The Hanged Man as someone the mob has "metaphorically hung" for their beliefs, and adds that "the message of the card is that the Seeker is right", not the mob. Voltaire writes this plot the other way round: Pangloss is hanged for his beliefs, but he was not right, and he does not back down. Later, already hanged, dissected by a surgeon and sent to the galleys, he says: "I am still of my first opinion… for I am a philosopher and I cannot retract." By then Candide has already defined this language: optimism, he says, "is the madness of maintaining that everything is right when it is wrong." And in the last chapter Voltaire adds one more stroke: Pangloss "asserted it still, though he no longer believed it" (et n'en croyait rien). **The Hanged Man at the entry, in its minus, is a shared slogan nobody has believed for a long time, but which it feels awkward to give up.**

One boundary. If "bearing it" in a couple means bearing threats, humiliation or violence, this is no longer the plot of a tail and not a lesson in patience. Then help is needed: a local emergency number or a crisis line.

sections.h2: Middle of the task: The Fool, or "we shall at least find new things"
paragraphs: Voltaire explains his hero's name in the very first paragraph: the young man "combined a true judgment with simplicity of spirit, which was the reason, I apprehend, of his being called Candide". In French, candide means "artless, guileless". This is The Fool: the card of someone who sets out into the world without knowing it and learns it the hard way. Waite calls The Fool "the spirit in search of experience", and the whole middle of the novel is the experience with which Candide tests Pangloss's lesson.

The middle of the book is a road. Candide goes through an army, a shipwreck, Lisbon, South America, Paris, Venice, while Cunegonde follows a route of her own. They are a couple — and apart almost the whole time. Lisovskaya's card lists this among The Fool's minuses as well: the couple seems to exist, yet does everything separately, and the status of the relationship is never settled.

The formula of the middle comes from Candide's servant Cacambo, when their strength has run out and an empty canoe turns up by a river: "let us … go with the current; a river always leads to some inhabited spot. If we do not find pleasant things we shall at least find new things." Candide agrees: "With all my heart … let us recommend ourselves to Providence." This is how a couple with The Fool in the middle travels their road. When things get hard, they do not clear the rubble; they change the place: a new city, a new job, a new project, "let's move, we'll sort it out there".

It is a real gift. Lisovskaya writes that Fool couples start from zero easily and find a way out of any problem; people see them as adventurers, and they have plenty of freedom and humour. Such a couple can lose almost everything and, six months later, be living in another city, laughing about how it all went. But the gift has a reverse side: **if every difficulty is solved by a road, the road becomes a way of not talking.**

sections.h2: El Dorado: the two happy ones resolved to be no longer so
paragraphs: The peak of the middle is El Dorado. The canoe passes under a vault of rock and carries Candide and Cacambo into a country where gold and gems lie on the roads instead of pebbles, and where there are no law courts and no prisons. Candide asks how people pray here. The old sage replies: "We do not pray to Him … we have nothing to ask of Him; He has given us all we need, and we return Him thanks without ceasing."

A month later Candide reasons: "If we abide here we shall only be upon a footing with the rest." But if they go home with even twelve sheep laden with the local pebbles, they will be richer than all the kings and will win Cunegonde back. Voltaire sums it up in one sentence: "mankind are so fond of roving, of making a figure in their own country, and of boasting of what they have seen in their travels, that the two happy ones resolved to be no longer so".

The King of El Dorado answers them with the word that opens Waite's divinatory list for The Fool: "You are foolish." The first word of that list is Folly, and the reversed list ends with vanity. Folly and vanity are exactly what the heroes take with them as they leave paradise. And the King adds a sentence that will turn out to be the main task of the whole book: **"when a person is comfortably settled in any part he should abide there"**.

The Fool's reversed list in Waite also contains a strange word, distribution, which Waite never explains. In Candide it comes true literally. Of the hundred and two sheep the King gave them, after a hundred days on the road only two remain: the rest sink in marshes, die in the desert, fall over precipices. What is left of the fortune goes on ransoms, gifts and swindlers. "You have rolled in millions of money, you and Cacambo," as Candide's companion Martin puts it. This is our reading, not Waite's interpretation: The Fool in the middle does not save, it gives away — generously and without counting.

For the 12-22-10 couple, El Dorado is the subtlest scene of the middle. The Fool can leave not only a bad place but a good one. Before the next "let's move", one question is worth asking: are we looking for something, or do we want to show something? Candide left paradise to arrive rich before Cunegonde — and by the end of the book all that remained of his riches was one small farm.

sections.h2: Main task: The Wheel of Fortune outside the farm windows
paragraphs: The third act opens with a sentence that could hang over any family celebration: "It is natural to imagine that after so many disasters Candide married … must have led a very happy life." The expectation does not come true. "His wife became uglier every day, more peevish and unsupportable", the old woman grew infirm, Pangloss despairs at not shining in some German university, Martin is sure that things are equally bad everywhere. Cacambo, who worked in the garden and took vegetables to sell in Constantinople, "was fatigued with hard work, and cursed his destiny". Note: the heroes already have a garden, and for now it does not save them.

In this chapter The Wheel of Fortune is visible literally. Boats full of pashas, effendis and cadis being sent into exile pass the farm, "and they saw other Cadis, Pashas, and Effendis coming to supply the place of the exiles, and afterwards exiled in their turn". The wheel turns right under the windows, while the house is quiet. And Voltaire records the central observation of the book: "Such spectacles as these increased the number of their dissertations; and when they did not dispute time hung so heavily upon their hands…"

That sentence is the Wheel's minus from Lisovskaya's card, written two and a half centuries before her: a swing between "silence and conflict". Either an argument or boredom; the people on the farm have no third option. And the old woman asks the question the whole book seems to have been written for: which is worse — all the miseries they have been through, "or to stay here and have nothing to do?" "It is a great question," says Candide. Martin concludes that "man was born to live either in a state of distracting inquietude or of lethargic disgust".

Here lies the secret of the 12-22-10 tail. **The first two cards prepare the couple for turns, and neither teaches them to stay.** The Hanged Man teaches them to wait it out, The Fool to pull up stakes and start again. While the wheel turns, the couple is in its element: it holds together through a move, a crisis, a strange city. When the wheel stops, such a couple often does not know what to do with calm and rocks it themselves — with a quarrel, a new move, a risky decision. From outside it looks as if "something is always happening to them". From inside it feels like boredom with nothing to fill it.

The main task D is read mostly through its minus — through what the couple fails at. For The Wheel, Lisovskaya writes of couples who blame fate and each other, hardly hear each other, and find it hard to be together while something still holds them. The task she sets is shared stability. Not calm as a reward for the storms survived, but the ability to live when there is no storm.

Waite mentions a manual of cartomancy that regards the whole deck "from beginning to end as the Wheel of Fortune", and does not object: such a description, he writes, "obtains in all the worlds". A novel about "the best of all possible worlds" tests exactly that: the wheel turns in Westphalia, in Lisbon and under the windows of a farm on the Propontis. The only thing that changes is what people do while it turns.

sections.h2: "All that is very well, but let us cultivate our garden"
paragraphs: Voltaire finds the way out not among philosophers. A famous dervish, asked by Pangloss why there is so much evil in the world, answers with a question: "When his highness sends a ship to Egypt, does he trouble his head whether the mice on board are at their ease or not?" To "What, then, must we do?" he replies in three words — "Hold your tongue" — and when Pangloss tries to go on about causes and effects, he shuts the door in their faces.

On the way home the heroes meet an old Turk taking the fresh air at his door under an orange bower. Two viziers and the mufti have just been strangled in the city, but the old man does not even know their names: "I content myself with sending there for sale the fruits of the garden which I cultivate." He has "only twenty acres", he works them with his children, and he explains: "our labour preserves us from three great evils—weariness, vice, and want." The first evil on that list — in Voltaire's French, ennui — is the very boredom that is choking Candide's farm.

Candide understands this before the philosophers do. He remarks that the old man "seems to be in a situation far preferable to that of the six kings with whom we had the honour of supping" in Venice — all six of them dethroned. Pangloss at once launches into a list of rulers thrown down by the wheel of fate, from Croesus and Caesar to Mary Stuart. Candide cuts him short: "I know also … that we must cultivate our garden." Martin agrees: "Let us work … without disputing; it is the only way to render life tolerable."

Then comes one of the warmest scenes in the book. "The whole little society entered into this laudable design, according to their different abilities." "Cunegonde was, indeed, very ugly, but she became an excellent pastry cook"; Paquette worked at embroidery, the old woman looked after the linen, and the former monk Friar Giroflée "made a good joiner, and became a very honest man". Three of Lisovskaya's pieces of advice for a Wheel couple meet here: accept your partner with their flaws, look for solutions instead of complaining, and do not shut yourselves away with each other. Candide's farm is not a couple behind four walls but a small society where everyone has their own work. The garden in which Cacambo cursed his destiny alone feeds everyone once they all take it on together.

The last page of the novel is a meeting of two ways of reading the Wheel. Pangloss says: "There is a concatenation of events in this best of all possible worlds: for if you had not been kicked out of a magnificent castle for love of Miss Cunegonde: if you had not been put into the Inquisition: if you had not walked over America: if you had not stabbed the Baron: if you had not lost all your sheep from the fine country of El Dorado: you would not be here eating preserved citrons and pistachio-nuts." And he hears in reply: "All that is very well," answered Candide, "but let us cultivate our garden."

Candide does not argue. He does not say that Pangloss was wrong and that it was all for nothing: he grants that it is well said — and goes back to work. For a 12-22-10 couple, this is the main task. The Hanged Man at the entry gives them the habit of justifying the past: none of it was in vain. The Wheel asks for something else. **Not winning the argument about fate — whether it was kind, whether the partner is to blame — but having shared work for the calm days.**

The circle of this tail looks like this. A lull sets in, and after a while it starts to feel cramped. One of the two suggests a change — that is The Fool. The change brings a turn of the wheel: a move, a crisis, a new bet. The couple gets through it on the common language of "let's bear it, it was meant to be" — that is The Hanged Man. A new lull sets in, and everything repeats. Simple, almost domestic things help break the circle.

ul: Notice the moment when "it was meant to be" is said instead of a decision. The scene with James is a reminder: an explanation offered instead of help is already a choice.
When a partner says "I feel awful", wine and oil first, theories later. The causes of the earthquake can wait.
Before every "let's move", ask the El Dorado question: are we looking for something, or do we want to prove something?
Give thanks rather than bargain with fate. The people of El Dorado ask for nothing and give thanks; Lisbon stages an auto-da-fé to buy safety, and the earth shakes again.
Set up your own "garden" for calm days in advance: shared work in which each has a role, from renovating a room to a small family project.
Do not lock the union up for two. Eight people live on Candide's farm, and it is everyone's work that saves it.
Answer arguments about the past with Candide's formula — "all that is very well, but…" — and move on to what can be done today.

paragraphs: The strong version of the tail is a couple who have been through change and come out of it not tired but skilled. Lisovskaya describes the Wheel in its plus as a sense of a fated meeting, a similar view of life, gratitude, and accepting the partner in any state. In Voltaire it is one line from the last page: "Their little plot of land produced plentiful crops." Not because the wheel stopped for ever, but because the couple at last has something to do while it stands still.

sections.h2: How the 12-22-10 tail adds up: an example with two dates
paragraphs: Each point of a couple's chart is the sum of the matching points of the two personal charts, reduced to 22. Take the dates 05.12.1976 and 14.05.1976. The first person's personal karmic tail is 3-7-22, the second's is 9-15-6. Add them point by point:

Entry: 3 + 9 = 12. Middle: 7 + 15 = 22. Main task: 22 + 6 = 28; the sum is above 22, so its digits are added, 2 + 8 = 10. The couple's centre for these dates is 8 + 3 = 11, Strength, and "The couple's values" hold The Lovers, 6.

Why no single person has this tail. In a personal chart the entry to the tail, M, is the sum of the main task D and the centre of the chart. For the entry to be 12 when D = 10, the centre would have to be 2, The High Priestess. A person's centre can only be 3–14, 16, 18, 20 or 22; 2 is not among them. So 12-22-10 is a tail for two only.

One more coincidence that is easy to mistake for a rule. In a personal tail the middle equals the reduced sum of the two ends, and here 12 + 10 = 22 as well. But in a couple the middle is not recalculated from the ends: the couple's Fool is the sum of the two personal middles, 7 + 15. The numbers coincide; the rule is different.

Four combinations of personal tails produce this same tail. Most often it is 3-7-22 with 9-15-6 (53% of such couples), less often 6-17-11 with 6-5-17 (42%), and quite rarely 3-13-10 with 9-9-18 (3%) or 6-14-8 with 6-8-20 (2%). These combinations show what the couple's cards are made of:

ul: **The couple's Fool is always the exact sum of the two personal middles:** 7 + 15, 17 + 5, 13 + 9 or 14 + 8. Reduction cannot produce 22: sums from 23 to 44 reduce to 12 at most. The couple does not borrow its road from one partner — the road only comes from the paths of both.

**Every couple's Wheel comes from 28:** 22 + 6, 11 + 17, 10 + 18 or 8 + 20. Only 3% bring a ready-made Wheel from a personal main task into the couple — the combination 3-13-10 with 9-9-18. In the most common case the Wheel is assembled from The Fool in one partner's main task and The Lovers in the other's.
**The Hanged Man at the entry is an exact sum too:** 3 + 9, The Empress and The Hermit (56% of couples), or 6 + 6, two Lovers (44%).

paragraphs: The 12-22-10 tail occurs in roughly one couple out of 269 (0.372%) and ranks 65th by frequency among the 97 couple tails.

sections.h2: Atmosphere and values: what stands next to the tail
paragraphs: Every couple with the 12-22-10 tail has one of two cards in the centre of their chart: Strength in 60.7% of cases or Judgement in 39.3%. The couple's centre governs the atmosphere inside the union — what happens between two people when nobody is watching.

Strength in the centre, for Lisovskaya, is a couple who sense finely what the other needs and charge each other with energy; in its minus each has their own truth, and they speak "different languages". For a tail that begins with a common language, this is an important neighbour: two different truths can live under one slogan, like Pangloss and Martin, who argue about metaphysics on the farm for years.

Judgement in the centre is cosiness, forgiving mistakes and support even when the partner is wrong. In its minus it is closedness: neither can say what they feel or what they dislike. In the novel, that is the wedding. "At the bottom of his heart Candide had no wish to marry Cunegonde", while "Cunegonde did not know she had grown ugly, for nobody had told her of it". The marriage is made between two silences.

"The couple's values" — what the union exists for — hold The Lovers (56.3%) or The Devil (43.7%) for these couples. For Lisovskaya, The Lovers in their plus include accepting the partner's imperfection. The road from the castle Pangloss called "the most magnificent of castles" to the pastry of a very plain Cunegonde is the road of this card. Lisovskaya's main thought about The Devil is that nobody belongs to anybody. Candide leaves El Dorado with his sheep to pay the governor for Cunegonde — in the French, "if Miss Cunegonde can be put at a price" (si mademoiselle Cunégonde peut être mise à prix; our translation) — and then "we will afterwards see what kingdom we shall be able to purchase". For a couple with The Devil in their values, this is an honest question to ask themselves: is one of the two trying to buy the other — with money, with sacrifice or with a debt of gratitude?

ul: **12 · The Hanged Man — entry to the task.** Where the couple begins and what they agree on without words: to wait, to give way, to explain every difficulty by "that's how it has to be". It is their shared wish and their shared brake.
**22 · The Fool — middle of the task.** How the couple travels their road: moves, changes, fresh starts from zero, readiness to pack up and go, and no certainty.
**10 · The Wheel of Fortune — main task.** What the couple has to learn: to take change without complaining about fate, and to get through calm times without boredom and quarrels.

intro: This tail comes with a ready-made plot. In 1759 Voltaire published Candide, or Optimism — the story of a young man and a young woman from one castle who are parted in the first chapter and married in the last. Between those chapters lie three acts, and they run exactly in the order 12-22-10. What follows is an investigation through that book, through the cards themselves and through the numbers of the couple's chart.

faq.q: Why does the 12-22-10 tail occur only in compatibility?
faq.a: In a personal chart the entry to the tail equals the sum of the main task and the centre. For the entry to be 12 when the main task is 10, the centre would have to be 2, and a person's centre can only be 3–14, 16, 18, 20 or 22. A couple's chart follows a different rule: each point is the sum of two personal ones, so 12-22-10 can come, for example, from the personal tails 3-7-22 and 9-15-6.

faq.q: What does "12 22 10 programme" mean in the destiny matrix?
faq.a: That is how this tail is often named in searches. For Lisovskaya, a couple's tail is the couple's "karmic programme": the tasks the union works through together. It is not a separate entity and not a verdict, but the same triple 12-22-10 read point by point: entry to the task, middle of the task, main task.

faq.q: Does The Wheel of Fortune promise a couple upheavals or luck?
faq.a: No. The numbers of the chart do not predict events, and The Wheel in the main task speaks not of misfortunes or windfalls but of how the couple relates to change. In Candide the earthquakes and shipwrecks are Voltaire's grotesque; what matches the cards is not the event but how the characters talk about it and what they do afterwards.

faq.q: Are there couple tails made of the same numbers in a different order?
faq.a: No. Among the 97 couple tails there is not a single permutation of 12, 22 and 10. The order 12-22-10 is the only one: The Hanged Man always at the entry, The Fool in the middle, The Wheel of Fortune in the main task.

faq.q: How is the couple's tail related to the partners' personal tails?
faq.a: The couple's tail is added up from the personal ones but read separately: the couple's points have their own meaning, and readings of a personal tail do not carry over to the couple. If one partner has the personal tail 3-7-22 and the other 9-15-6, each has a plot of their own, while 12-22-10 describes what arises only between them.

report: Voltaire's Candide, or Optimism ends not with a wedding but with boredom. Candide and Cunegonde have been through a shipwreck, an earthquake, half the world and a long separation; at last they settle together on a small farm — and discover that calm is harder for them than disaster. The three cards of the 12-22-10 tail run in the same order as the three acts of the book: The Hanged Man, The Fool, The Wheel of Fortune.

The lovers grew up on the lessons of the philosopher Pangloss, whose name is built from the Greek words pan, "all", and glossa, "tongue" or "language". The point where a 12-22-10 couple has The Hanged Man carries two labels in the reading: "Entry to the task" and "Common language". This couple's common language is Pangloss's: "they should have said all is for the best". Let's bear it, let's wait, it was meant to be.

This is the language in which the couple enters its task. Candide and Cunegonde name their wish in the first chapter — a kiss behind a screen — and in the same minute it is suspended for the rest of the book: the Baron throws the young man out of the castle. The wedding comes only in the last chapter, and even then from a push from outside: "the extreme impertinence of the Baron determined him to conclude the match". In real life it shows in small things. The wedding is put off "until we have our own flat", the move "until the promotion", the important conversation "until the holidays".

The Hanged Man has two sides here. It gives the couple tact and the ability to wait and to give way. But the entry point stands on the line of tasks, and the same wish turns into resistance. Voltaire shows this in Lisbon harbour. A sailor "tumbled head foremost overboard, and stuck upon a piece of the broken mast"; good James hauls him up and drowns himself. Candide is about to jump after him, "but was prevented by the philosopher Pangloss, who demonstrated to him that the Bay of Lisbon had been made on purpose for the Anabaptist to be drowned". **A common language that explains every loss sooner or later starts explaining inaction too.**

report.h3: A bargain with fate that buys nothing

report: After the earthquake the sages of the country decide to calm the tremors with an auto-da-fé. Candide is flogged, Pangloss is hanged. Voltaire's next sentence: "The same day the earth sustained a most violent concussion." In one scene the first and the last cards of the tail meet: a sacrifice is made to stop the Wheel, and the Wheel keeps turning. Our reading is a secret bargain with fate: "if we endure it properly, we will be repaid". Even in the novel it buys nothing. Pangloss himself, hanged and sent to the galleys, does not retract his views, and in the last chapter, as Voltaire puts it, "asserted it still, though he no longer believed it".
One boundary: if "bearing it" in a couple means bearing threats, humiliation or violence, this is no longer the plot of a tail. Then help is needed — a local emergency number or a crisis line.

report.h3: "We shall at least find new things"

report: The middle of the novel is a road, and The Fool is at work in it. Voltaire explains his hero's name like this: the young man "combined a true judgment with simplicity of spirit, which was the reason, I apprehend, of his being called Candide". The formula of the middle comes from his servant Cacambo beside an empty canoe: "If we do not find pleasant things we shall at least find new things." This is how a 12-22-10 couple gets through hard places: it does not clear the rubble, it changes the place. It is a real gift — starting from zero with ease. Until the road becomes a way of not talking.

The subtlest scene of the middle is El Dorado, a country where gold lies on the roads and nobody asks God for anything, only gives thanks. A month later Candide reasons: "If we abide here we shall only be upon a footing with the rest." Voltaire sums it up: "the two happy ones resolved to be no longer so". The King calls this folly — the very word that opens Waite's divinatory list for The Fool. And he adds a sentence that will turn out to be the main task of the whole book: **"when a person is comfortably settled in any part he should abide there"**. The Fool can leave not only a bad place but a good one.

The third act is the farm by the Propontis. Here The Wheel of Fortune is visible literally: boats carrying exiled pashas and cadis pass by, and "other Cadis, Pashas, and Effendis" come "to supply the place of the exiles, and afterwards exiled in their turn". The wheel turns under the windows, the house is quiet, and Voltaire records: "Such spectacles as these increased the number of their dissertations; and when they did not dispute time hung so heavily upon their hands…" This is the Wheel's minus — a swing between silence and conflict. The old woman asks which is worse: all the miseries they have survived, "or to stay here and have nothing to do?" "It is a great question," says Candide.

This is the secret of the tail. **The first two cards prepare the couple for turns, and neither teaches them to stay.** The Hanged Man teaches them to wait it out, The Fool to pull up stakes and start again. While the wheel turns, the couple holds together through a move, a crisis, a strange city. When the wheel stops, such a couple often does not know what to do with calm and rocks it themselves: with a quarrel, a new move, a risky decision. The main task is shared stability. Not calm as a reward for the storms survived, but the ability to live when there is no storm.

report.h3: "All that is very well, but let us cultivate our garden"

report: The way out comes from an old Turk who does not even know the names of the viziers just strangled in the city. He has "only twenty acres", he works them with his children, and "our labour preserves us from three great evils—weariness, vice, and want". Weariness — in Voltaire's French, ennui — comes first on that list. The people of the farm take up the work together, "according to their different abilities". "Cunegonde was, indeed, very ugly, but she became an excellent pastry cook." The partner is accepted with their flaws, and the union is not locked up for two: eight people live on the farm, and it is everyone's work that saves it.

The last page is a meeting of two ways of reading the Wheel. Pangloss proves that none of it was in vain: without the expulsion from the castle, the Inquisition and the sheep lost from El Dorado, there would be no candied citrons and pistachios on the table now. The answer comes: "All that is very well," answered Candide, "but let us cultivate our garden." **Not winning the argument about fate, but having shared work for the calm days** — that is the strong version of the 12-22-10 tail.
